summary: This experimental memo defines how to use SPX, a public-key authentication system, within the Telnet authentication option. It is one of several authentication types Telnet could negotiate.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1412 defines how a Telnet connection can use SPX to check a user's identity. One side sends an authentication token, and the other accepts or rejects it; they can also check each other.

subtitle: A Telnet authentication exchange using SPX tokens.

tldr.problem: Telnet's authentication option needs a defined exchange for SPX authentication tokens.
tldr.mechanism: The client or server sends an AUTH command with an SPX token. The other side replies with ACCEPT or REJECT; ACCEPT can include a mutual-authentication response.
tldr.outcome: The Experimental RFC defines how SPX fits the Telnet authentication option and how both sides establish an 8-byte key for the Telnet Encryption option.

today: RFC 1412 defines an Experimental Telnet authentication mechanism. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: SPX in the Telnet Authentication Option
sections.content:
RFC 1412 assigns the name SPX and type code 3 to this authentication method. It specifies how SPX tokens use Telnet's existing authentication option; it does not define the token's internal syntax, which the RFC says will be described elsewhere.

After an SPX exchange, the two sides have securely established a random 8-byte key for use as the default key with Telnet's Encryption option.
sections.plainLanguage: SPX is one authentication method that Telnet can negotiate. The RFC defines how Telnet carries its token, while leaving the token's format to another document.

sections.title: The Authentication Messages
sections.content:
AUTH carries the SPX authentication token. A successful exchange ends with ACCEPT; an unsuccessful one ends with REJECT, which may include an ASCII reason message.

When mutual authentication is requested, ACCEPT carries a mutual response for the receiver to compare with its expected response. With one-way authentication, the response contains zero bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender provides its SPX token, and the other side reports success or failure. If both sides are checking identities, the accepting side also sends a response token.

sections.title: Who Starts and What Happens Next
sections.content:
The AUTH_WHO modifier determines who sends the first AUTH command. With AUTH_WHO_CLIENT, the client starts and the server replies; with AUTH_WHO_SERVER, the server starts and the client replies.

Every later authentication command must keep the same modifiers as the first command. Authentication identifies the user, but authorization is a separate decision: the server checks account access after authentication finishes and can still deny access.
sections.plainLanguage: A modifier tells Telnet which side starts, and later messages keep the same settings. Passing the identity check does not guarantee access to an account; the server decides that separately.

sections.title: A Risk During Negotiation
sections.content:
The RFC warns that choosing an authentication method happens before authentication has occurred. At that point, neither system knows whether it is speaking to the intended system.

An intruder could try to negotiate a weak authentication system or one the intruder has already compromised. The RFC says this negotiation feature should be used with caution.
sections.plainLanguage: The systems choose an authentication method before either has proved its identity. An attacker could try to make them choose a weak or compromised method.
